stimuli.text: A block of mass 2 kg on a 37° incline is connected by a light string over a light, frictionless pulley at the top of the incline to a hanging block of mass 3 kg. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is 0.15. The system is released from rest, and the hanging block descends.
A block of mass 0.4 kg on a horizontal frictionless surface is attached to a spring. Its position is $$x(t) = 0.08\cos(7t)$$, with x in meters and t in seconds.
Students measure the period of a simple pendulum for several string lengths, using small amplitudes.
A hoop (I = MR²) and a solid sphere (I = ⅖MR²) of equal mass M and radius R are released from rest at the top of the same ramp of height 1.5 m. Both roll without slipping.

questions.stem: A car moving at 20 m/s brakes with a constant deceleration of 6 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping?

options.why: Δx = v₀²/(2a).
Divide by 2a, not a.
Correct. Use v² = v₀² + 2aΔx with v = 0.
That is the stopping time in seconds.

questions.stem: A car rounds a flat curve of radius 120 m. The coefficient of static friction is 0.6. What is the maximum speed without skidding?

options.why: Take the square root.
Include the friction coefficient.
Correct. Static friction supplies the centripetal force: μmg = mv²/r.
μ multiplies g r.

questions.stem: A motor lifts a 340 kg load 8 m at constant speed in 18 s. What average power does it deliver?

options.why: P = W/t.
Correct. P = mgh/t.
That is the work; divide by time.
Include g.

questions.stem: A particle's position is $$x(t) = -1t^3 - 6t^2 - 1t$$, with x in meters and t in seconds. What is its acceleration at $$t = 1$$ s?

options.why: Bring each exponent down as a factor when differentiating.
That is the velocity; differentiate again.
The derivative of 2bt is 2b, which also remains.
Correct. Differentiate twice: a = 6at + 2b.

questions.explanation: a(t) = -6t - 12, so at t = 1 the value is -18.

questions.stem: A 1.9 kg mass oscillates on a spring with $$k = 85$$ N/m. What is the period?

options.why: Include the 2π.
Correct. T = 2π√(m/k).
That is the frequency.
The ratio is m/k.

questions.stem: A boat points straight across a river 140 m wide, moving at 3 m/s relative to the water. The current flows at 2 m/s. How far downstream does the boat land?

options.why: Correct. The current does not change the time to cross; it only carries the boat downstream.
Use the crossing time w/v_boat.
Drift = current speed × crossing time.
That is a time, not a distance.

questions.stem: Two springs with constants 30 N/m and 90 N/m are connected in parallel and support a 0.5 kg mass at rest. How far do they stretch in total?

options.why: Correct. k_eq = k₁ + k₂.
Both springs share the load.
The force is the weight, mg.
Series and parallel rules are reversed.

questions.stem: A 0.1 kg ball hits a wall at 18 m/s and rebounds at 14 m/s. The contact lasts 0.03 s. What is the average force from the wall?

options.why: Include the rebound.
Correct. Δp = m(v_f − v_i) with the direction reversed.
Divide by time.
The velocity reverses, so the speeds add.

questions.stem: A planet has 3 times Earth's mass and 2 times Earth's radius. What is the gravitational field strength at its surface? (Earth's is 9.8 N/kg.)

options.why: The ratio is inverted.
g decreases with radius.
g depends on 1/R², not 1/R.
Correct. g ∝ M/R².

questions.stem: A spring with $$k = 270$$ N/m is compressed 0.18 m and launches a 0.6 kg block across a frictionless surface. What is the block's speed after leaving the spring?

options.why: Correct. ½kx² = ½mv².
Take the square root.
The ½ appears on both sides.
Use energy: v = x√(k/m).

questions.stem: A block slides down a 20° incline. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.15. What is the magnitude of its acceleration?

options.why: Correct. a = g(sin θ − μk cos θ).
Friction acts up the slope.
The component along the incline is mg sin θ.
Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.

questions.stem: Masses of 9 kg and 7 kg hang on either side of a light, frictionless pulley. What is the magnitude of their acceleration?

options.why: The masses are connected, so a is less than g.
Correct. a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂).
The fraction is inverted.
The whole system accelerates: divide by both masses.

questions.stem: A 2 kg cart moving at 2 m/s collides with and sticks to a 7 kg cart at rest. What is their speed after the collision?

options.why: Kinetic energy is not conserved here.
Correct. Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not.
The carts share the momentum.
Use m₁v₁ for the initial momentum.

questions.explanation: v_f = 2·2/9 = 0.444 m/s; kinetic energy lost = 3.11 J.

questions.stem: A ball rolls off a horizontal ledge 15 m high at 8 m/s. How far from the base of the ledge does it land?

options.why: Take the square root for the time.
Correct. Fall time from the height, times the horizontal speed.
Fall time is √(2h/g).
Horizontal and vertical motion are independent.

questions.stem: A wheel spinning at 48 rad/s slows uniformly to rest in 12 s. How many revolutions does it make while stopping?

options.why: Correct. Δθ = ½ω₀t, then divide by 2π.
That is in radians; convert to revolutions.
The average angular speed is ω₀/2.
Recheck the average.

questions.stem: A simple pendulum is 2 m long. What is its period for small oscillations?

options.why: Take the square root.
Include 2π.
The ratio is L/g.
Correct. T = 2π√(L/g).

questions.stem: A 59 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator that is accelerating upward at 1 m/s². What does the scale read?

options.why: Check the direction of the acceleration.
The acceleration changes the normal force.
Correct. The scale reads the normal force: N − mg = ma (up positive).
Include gravity.

questions.stem: A system obeys $$\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -81x$$. What is the period of its motion?

options.why: T = 2π/ω, not 2πω.
ω is the square root of the coefficient.
Correct. ω = √81 = 9 rad/s, T = 2π/ω.
T = 2π/ω.

questions.stem: A 2 kg ball moving at +3 m/s collides elastically head-on with a 7 kg ball at rest. What is the velocity of the 7 kg ball afterward (positive in the original direction)?

options.why: Only equal masses exchange velocities.
Kinetic energy is conserved too.
That would be a sticking collision.
Correct. Elastic: conserve momentum and kinetic energy (relative velocity reverses).

questions.explanation: v₁' = (m₁ − m₂)v/(m₁ + m₂) = -1.67 m/s; v₂' = 2m₁v/(m₁ + m₂) = 1.33 m/s.

questions.stem: A 12 g bullet moving at 290 m/s embeds in a 3.5 kg block hanging from strings. How high does the block rise?

options.why: Correct. Momentum for the collision, then energy for the swing.
Kinetic energy is not conserved in the collision.
Find the block's speed after the collision first.
h = V²/(2g).

questions.explanation: V = 0.991 m/s after the collision; h = V²/(2g) = 0.0501 m.

questions.stem: A ball is launched from level ground at 17 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, what is its time of flight?

options.why: Correct. Treat horizontal and vertical motion separately.
Use v₀ sin θ.
Use the vertical component.
That is the time to the top; the flight is twice as long.

questions.explanation: v₀x = 14.7 m/s, v₀y = 8.5 m/s. T = 2v₀y/g = 1.73 s.

questions.stem: A mass on a spring oscillates with angular frequency 7 rad/s and amplitude 0.14 m. What is its speed when it is 0.028 m from equilibrium?

options.why: Correct. v = ω√(A² − x²), from conservation of energy.
Use A² − x² under a square root.
That is the maximum speed, at x = 0.
Speed is greatest at equilibrium, not at the ends.

questions.stem: A 3 kg object at rest experiences a net force $$F(t) = 7t$$ N from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 4$$ s. What is its final speed?

options.why: Integrate the force over time.
The force is not constant.
Correct. Impulse ∫F dt equals the change in momentum.
Divide by the mass to get speed.

questions.explanation: J = ∫F dt = 56 N·s; v = J/m = 18.7 m/s.

questions.stem: A block starts from rest and slides 6 m down a 37° incline with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.1. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Friction removes energy.
Use the vertical drop, L sin θ.
Correct. mgh − μmg cos θ·L = ½mv².
Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.

questions.stem: A 7 kg block on a horizontal table is connected by a string over a light pulley to a hanging 4 kg block. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the table and the block is 0.2. What is the acceleration of the blocks?

options.why: Correct. Net force (m₂g − μm₁g) divided by the total mass.
Both blocks accelerate; divide by the total mass.
Friction opposes the motion.
Include friction on the table block.

questions.stem: A 5 kg mass hangs from a light string wrapped around a uniform disk pulley of mass 6 kg that turns on a frictionless axle. What is the acceleration of the mass?

options.why: For a disk, I/R² = M/2.
I/R² = M/2.
Correct. a = mg/(m + M/2), using I = ½MR² and a = Rα.
The pulley's inertia reduces the acceleration.

questions.explanation: mg − T = ma and TR = ½MR²(a/R) give a = 6.13 m/s².

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 1 m is pivoted at one end and released from rest in a horizontal position. What is its angular acceleration just after release?

options.why: Correct. τ = Mg(L/2) and I = ML²/3 give α = 3g/(2L).
The weight acts at L/2.
Use τ = Iα with I = ML²/3.
τ = MgL/2.

questions.stem: A rod lies along the x-axis from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 2$$ m and has linear mass density $$\lambda = kx^3$$. Where is its center of mass?

options.why: Integrate x·xⁿ and xⁿ correctly.
The rod is not uniform.
Correct. x_cm = ∫xλ dx / ∫λ dx.
The exponents are n + 2 and n + 1.

questions.stem: What is the rotational inertia of a uniform rod of mass 7 kg and length 1 m about an axis through one end, perpendicular to the rod?

options.why: Correct. I = ML²/3 (parallel-axis theorem from ML²/12).
That is about the center.
The mass is spread along the rod.
That is a disk's formula.

questions.stem: A force $$F(x) = 6x^2$$ N acts along the x-axis. How much work does it do on an object moving from $$x = 1$$ m to $$x = 4$$ m?

options.why: The force is not constant.
Divide by n + 1 when integrating.
Correct. W = ∫F dx.
Integrate; do not just evaluate F.

questions.stem: A thin spherical shell rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp of height 2.7 m. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Some energy goes into rotation.
Rotational energy is ½Iω² = ½βmv².
That is only correct for a hoop.
Correct. mgh = ½mv²(1 + β) with I = ⅔MR².

questions.stem: A planet has mass $$7 \times 10^{24}$$ kg and radius $$2 \times 10^{7}$$ m. What is the escape speed from its surface? ($$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$$ N·m²/kg²)

options.why: Correct. ½mv² = GMm/R.
That is the circular orbit speed; escape needs √2 times more.
Take the square root.
Potential energy uses 1/R.

questions.stem: A block starts from rest and slides 2 m down a 30° incline with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.3. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Use the vertical drop, L sin θ.
Correct. mgh − μmg cos θ·L = ½mv².
Friction removes energy.
Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.

questions.explanation: h = 1 m. v = √(2g(h − μL cos θ)) = 3.07 m/s.

questions.stem: A constant torque of 20 N·m acts on a wheel ($$I = 0.2$$ kg·m²) initially at rest, through 4 revolutions. What is the wheel's final angular speed?

options.why: ½Iω² = W; solve for ω.
Correct. Work τΔθ (in radians) equals ½Iω².
W = ½Iω².
Convert revolutions to radians.

questions.stem: A 3000 kg car heading east at 9 m/s collides with a 2000 kg car heading north at 16 m/s, and they lock together. What is their speed just after the collision?

options.why: Weight each velocity by its mass.
Correct. Conserve momentum in x and y separately, then combine.
Momentum is a vector; add components at right angles.
Divide by the total mass.

questions.stem: Satellite B orbits a planet in a circular orbit 4 times the radius of satellite A's circular orbit. What is the ratio of B's orbital period to A's?

options.why: Correct. T² ∝ r³, so T ∝ r^(3/2).
Kepler's third law: T ∝ r^(3/2).
T² ∝ r³.
The exponent is 3/2.

questions.stem: The potential energy of a particle is $$U(x) = 4x^3 - 18x$$ J. At what positive x is the particle in stable equilibrium?

options.why: Correct. Equilibrium where dU/dx = 0; stable at a minimum.
Take the square root.
dU/dx = 3ax² − b.
Set the derivative, not U, to zero.

questions.explanation: dU/dx = 12x² − 18 = 0 gives x = 1.22 m; d²U/dx² > 0 there, so it is stable.

questions.stem: A 2 kg ball on a 0.9 m string moves in a vertical circle. At the bottom of the circle its speed is 5 m/s. What is the tension in the string there?

options.why: Correct. At the bottom, T − mg = mv²/r.
Check the direction of gravity relative to the center.
Centripetal force uses v².
Include gravity.

questions.stem: A uniform 8 m beam weighing 600 N rests on supports at both ends. A 700 N load sits 7 m from the left end. What force does the right support exert?

options.why: The load is not at the center.
Correct. Take torques about the left support.
Include the beam's weight at its center.
That is the left support's force.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 3 kg and radius 0.3 m spins at 19 rad/s on a frictionless axle. A 0.75 kg lump of clay is dropped onto the rim and sticks. What is the new angular speed?

options.why: The clay's inertia is mR².
Correct. Angular momentum is conserved: I_iω_i = I_fω_f.
Kinetic energy is not conserved in a sticking collision.
Use rotational inertias, not masses.

questions.title: Block on an incline with a hanging mass

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a free-body diagram for the 2 kg block, labeling each force.

rubric.criterion: Weight down, normal force perpendicular to the incline, tension up the incline.
Kinetic friction down the incline (opposite the motion).

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the acceleration of the system in terms of the masses, θ, μ and g, then calculate its value.

rubric.criterion: Newton's second law applied to each block (or the system).

parts.prompt: Calculate the tension in the string.
Calculate the speed of the blocks after the hanging block has descended 0.5 m, and the work done by friction on the incline block during that motion.

rubric.criterion: Work by friction, with a negative sign.

parts.prompt: Sketch (describe) graphs of position, velocity and acceleration versus time for one period, aligned vertically.

rubric.criterion: Position is a cosine starting at +A; velocity is a negative sine starting at 0.
rubric.example: x starts at 0.08 m; v starts at 0 and goes negative.

rubric.criterion: Acceleration starts at its negative maximum and is opposite in sign to position throughout.

parts.prompt: Derive expressions for v(t) and a(t), and determine the maximum speed and maximum acceleration.
Calculate the spring constant and the period.
Calculate the total mechanical energy and describe how kinetic and potential energy vary during one period.

rubric.example: K is maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±A; U is the reverse; the sum is constant. Each varies twice per period.

parts.prompt: Describe a procedure the students could use to measure the period accurately, including how to reduce uncertainty.

rubric.example: Time 10 swings with a stopwatch and divide by 10.

rubric.criterion: Keep the amplitude small and repeat trials.
rubric.example: Release from under about 10° and average several trials.

parts.prompt: Identify quantities to graph that would give a straight line, and explain how g can be found from the graph.
Plot (describe) the linearized data and draw a best-fit line. Use it to calculate an experimental value of g.
The students repeat the experiment with a much larger amplitude. Predict how the measured periods would change and explain.

rubric.criterion: Periods increase slightly; the small-angle approximation (sin θ ≈ θ) no longer holds.
rubric.example: The restoring torque is less than proportional to θ at large angles.

parts.prompt: Without calculating, predict which object reaches the bottom first. Justify your prediction using energy.

rubric.example: It has the smaller rotational inertia per MR².

rubric.criterion: Justification: less of its energy goes into rotation, so more is translational kinetic energy.

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed at the bottom of an object with rotational inertia βMR², in terms of g, h and β.

rubric.criterion: Energy conservation including both forms of kinetic energy, with v = Rω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of each object at the bottom.
Explain whether your derived expression is consistent with your prediction in part (a), and why neither speed depends on M or R.

rubric.criterion: Smaller β gives larger v, consistent with the prediction.
M and R cancel in the energy equation.
rubric.example: Only the shape factor β matters.
